strengths: The demonstrated accuracy–latency tradeoff supports weak acceptance. NCI requires only O(P) additional computation after classification and avoids storing a training-feature bank. Table 1b reports latency essentially matching MSP: 0.54 versus 0.53 ms on CIFAR-10 and 6.84 versus 6.85 ms on ImageNet.

The evaluation covers three ID datasets and four architecture families, with both AUROC and FPR95 reported. Table 3 shows average AUROC of 88.57 versus 86.80 for Scale. The Swin-v2 results are particularly useful: NCI achieves 80.97 AUROC versus 76.71 for Scale, supporting its value beyond any single benchmark.

The component ablations demonstrate useful complementarity. On ImageNet ResNet-50, Table 6 reports 88.56 AUROC for NCI versus 84.41 for proximity alone, 78.91 for the L1 norm alone, and 86.37 for KNN plus L1. Table 7 also supports the proposed weight-norm adjustment over plain cosine similarity.

The detector is simple, operates on existing classifiers without retraining, and has an explicit scoring formula. Per-dataset results, checkpoint sources, supplementary implementation details, and a code link aid inspection and reproduction.
weaknesses: The proposed explanation for feature-norm separation is not established. Sections 3.1–3.3 argue that forming a simplex ETF requires features to lie sufficiently far from the origin, but ETF angles and equal-norm structure are preserved under arbitrary common rescaling. Moreover, the ETF concerns centered features, whereas the filter uses uncentered feature norms. Neural collapse alone therefore does not explain the claimed absolute ID–OOD norm separation. This is a substantive limitation of the conceptual contribution, although the empirical benefit of the filter remains supported.

Theorem 3.1 is stronger than its proof. Equation (4) establishes convergence of a normalized discrepancy; obtaining the unnormalized convergence in Equation (2) additionally requires control of class-mean norm growth or an appropriate convergence-rate condition. Those assumptions are absent, so the theorem is not justified as stated.

The evidence attributing the gains specifically to neural collapse is limited. Figures 1–2 examine CIFAR-10 versus SVHN, while Appendix 13 reproduces training diagnostics from prior work rather than measuring collapse in the evaluated checkpoints. Also, pScore simplifies to w_c^T(h−μ_G)/||h−μ_G||₂, but no ablation isolates centering against the corresponding uncentered score. Thus, the experiments establish score effectiveness more convincingly than the claimed mechanism or the necessity of centering.

Some comparative claims need qualification. Table 2 omits closely related NECO and fDBD, limiting conclusions about superiority across architectures. In Table 4, using the same coefficient grid for differently scaled L1, L2, and L-infinity norms does not ensure equally effective tuning, so the claimed intrinsic advantage of L1 is less firmly established.

Reporting gaps affect reproducibility more than the core method: the Gaussian validation-set size, preprocessing, and selection objective are insufficiently specified. Timing details such as batching and synchronization are also missing, and the ImageNet KNN latency is imported from another paper. These limitations weaken precise speedup comparisons, while leaving the low-complexity argument credible.
